summary: An engineering spec is a contract. It says WHAT a system, component, endpoint, or message must do — independent of HOW it is implemented.

facts.text: An engineering spec is a contract. It says WHAT a system, component, endpoint, or message must do - independent of HOW it is implemented.
Three forms dominate modern practice:
API specs - machine-readable contracts for HTTP (OpenAPI 3.1) and event-driven (AsyncAPI 3.0) interfaces
Behavior specs - executable narratives (Gherkin / Given-When-Then)
Data specs - schema contracts (JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf)

Joel Spolsky's 2000 series "Painless Functional Specifications" introduced the discipline: a functional spec describes how a product works from the user's perspective; a technical spec describes internal implementation.
A spec that says "internally we'll use a Redis cache with 5-minute TTL" has leaked implementation.
Litmus test: If you could swap out the implementation entirely and the spec still holds, the spec is at the right level.
Contract-first development: agree on the contract before writing code. The OpenAPI / AsyncAPI document is the source of truth.
Key top-level fields:
openapi - version (3.1.0)
info - name, version, description
servers - base URLs per environment
paths - endpoints, verbs, parameters, request/response shapes
components - reusable schemas, parameters, responses, security schemes
YAML is preferred over JSON for human authoring.
Key concepts in v3.0:
Channels are addressable destinations (Kafka topic, AMQP queue) - decoupled from operations
Operations describe what an application does on a channel using action: send or action: receive
Messages are defined once and referenced from channels and operations
Use Gherkin for: business-logic behavior (pricing rules, eligibility checks, state transitions), workflows spanning multiple systems.
Avoid Gherkin for: API shape (use OpenAPI), data format (use JSON Schema).
A spec is a promise. Once published:
Versioning - non-breaking changes bump minor; breaking changes bump major.
Backward compatibility - additive changes (new optional field) are safe; removals, renames, type changes are breaking.
Deprecation policy - published timeline (e.g., 12 months notice for major version sunset).
URL versioning (/v1/users) - explicit, cacheable
Date-pinned versioning (Stripe: Stripe-Version: 2024-04-10) - fine-grained
Version in the topic name (orders.v1, orders.v2)
Schema registry with explicit compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL)

facets.title: 8. Examples are part of the spec

facts.text: OpenAPI's examples field and Gherkin's Examples: table are not decorative - they are the spec. CI tools validate that examples conform to the declared schema.
Implementation leakage - spec mentions Redis, Postgres, language choice.
No examples - schemas without concrete payloads.
Hand-waved errors - "returns an error on failure" without listing codes.
Missing versioning policy.
Spec-test drift - spec says one thing, implementation does another, no CI check.
Optional everything - every field is optional, every status code is default.
Joel Spolsky, "Painless Functional Specifications, Part 2"
OpenAPI Specification v3.1: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0
AsyncAPI 3.0.0 Specification: https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.0.0
Cucumber, "Gherkin Reference": https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/
Writing an HTTP API contract before implementation begins, using OpenAPI 3.1 so client and server teams can build against the same source of truth in parallel.

facts.text: Use Gherkin for cross-system behavioral rules and reserve OpenAPI/JSON Schema for API shape and data format — don't try to make one tool do both jobs.

facts.text: A spec is only as trustworthy as its examples; if CI doesn't validate that examples conform to the declared schema, the spec and the running system can silently drift apart.

facts.text: Gherkin captures behavior well but says nothing about API shape or data format — a team that tries to spec an HTTP interface entirely in Given-When-Then loses the machine-readable contract OpenAPI provides.

facts.text: Once a spec is published, it becomes a promise to every consumer; even a well-intentioned cleanup of a poorly-designed field now requires a version bump and a migration path rather than a quiet fix.
